sections.title: Recognition
sections.text: The European chanterelle has a yellow to yellow-orange cap, about 3–12 cm across, whose margin becomes wavy and whose centre can become depressed. Its underside carries thick, blunt, forked ridges that run down the stem; these are folds of the fruiting body, not thin true gills. The solid, smooth stem is close to the cap in colour. Flesh is pale and the fresh mushroom often has a fruity, apricot-like smell.

sections.title: Habitat and season
sections.text: This mycorrhizal fungus fruits on the ground under broadleaved or coniferous trees, sometimes in groups. In European woodland it appears mainly from summer to late autumn; local weather shifts the season. The spore deposit is pale cream to yellowish.

sections.title: Confusions
sections.text: Hygrophoropsis aurantiaca has thin, crowded true gills rather than thick blunt folds. The toxic Omphalotus olearius has true gills and commonly grows in clusters on wood or buried roots. A stem arising from apparently bare soil does not by itself rule out buried wood; inspect the attachment and all underside characters.

sections.title: Food safety
sections.text: Cantharellus cibarius is considered edible, but a drawing or one feature cannot confirm a harvest. Only use specimens identified with certainty and cook them adequately. Seek expert advice if the folds, habitat or full specimen cannot be assessed.

traits: Yellow to orange-yellow cap with a wavy, sometimes funnel-shaped margin
Thick blunt forked folds run down the stem; no true gills
Solid smooth stem in a similar colour to the cap
Pale flesh and often a fruity smell
On soil with trees; pale cream-yellow spore print
safetyNote: Edible only after reliable identification. The toxic Omphalotus olearius has true gills and grows on wood or buried roots; do not rely on colour alone. Cook identified specimens and obtain expert advice when uncertain.
